note: A container written by a conforming writer, byte for byte. This is the only case in the corpus that pins section 7.1's whole writer table at once, and the only one that pins its entry-order rule at all. Two independent implementations produce these exact 562 bytes for this document and these three attachments, sha256 2e7cc0cfa3337b85e3bc2053fb9c4cb355dcbdd036a74ec4d284b18bacd128c5. THE ENTRY LIST IS CHOSEN AND NOT TIDY, and it is the load-bearing part of the case. `Ｚ.txt` begins U+FF3A and `😀.txt` begins U+1F600. By code point U+FF3A sorts first; by UTF-16 code unit U+1F600 sorts first, because its high surrogate begins at U+D800, which is below U+FF3A. Section 7.1 requires code-point order, so a writer using its language's default string comparison emits these two the wrong way round and fails - while every ASCII-only set of names passes under either comparator. If the attachment set is ever reduced, keep one name above U+FFFF beside one in U+E000 to U+FFFF, or the case stops testing the ordering rule and only tests that some attachments round-trip. Three further properties, each of which a change to the fixture could silently remove. The bytes are reproducible only because 7.1 fixes every header field, including the 1980-01-01 timestamp, and forbids deflate: deflate has no canonical output, so a single deflated entry would make this case reproducible in one language only and it would fail everywhere else for a reason that is not the writer's fault. The archive must be produced through the WRITE path, never by repackaging a decoded container, which is a re-render and reproduces what the input carried instead of applying the emit-boundary rules. And the writer must sort its own entries rather than trusting the order it was handed: verified by passing these three attachments in REVERSED order and getting the same 562 bytes, so a runner may feed them in any order and a writer that preserved input order would fail. The attachments are carried in a JSON manifest rather than as real files beside this sidecar, deliberately: a name holding U+1F600 is subject to filesystem Unicode normalisation and case folding, so a checked-out file could differ from the name the case means. Inside JSON the name is escaped text and no filesystem can alter it.
